title: FROM VISIBILITY TO PREDICTION: CAN SUPPLY CHAIN SEE RISK BEFORE IT BECOMES DELAY?
excerpt: By the time a material appears on a late-delivery report, the most useful part of the story may already be over. The supplier may have slipped weeks earlier, an approval may have consumed the schedule buffer, or an inspection window may have quietly moved.
imageAlt: FROM VISIBILITY TO PREDICTION: CAN SUPPLY CHAIN SEE RISK BEFORE IT BECOMES DELAY?
bodyHtml:
By the time a material appears on a late-delivery report, the most useful part of the story may already be over. The supplier may have slipped weeks earlier, an approval may have consumed the schedule buffer, or an inspection window may have quietly moved. The real opportunity is earlier: noticing that the pattern is changing while there are still practical choices.

Executive Insight

Article 6 looked at the gap between process performance and the final business outcome. A workflow can appear healthy while waiting time between functions quietly pushes material toward delay. This article moves one step further. Once those handoffs and milestones are visible, can we use them to recognize risk before the required date is actually missed?

In practice, the warning signs are often already there. A supplier moves a fabrication milestone twice. Technical approval takes longer than normal. Inspection dates become tighter. Logistics loses part of its contingency. Inventory is being consumed faster than expected. Each signal may look manageable on its own; together, they can tell a very different story.

This is what I mean by prediction here. Not a system claiming to know the future, but an organization becoming better at noticing change early enough to do something about it.

Why Early Warning Matters More Than Early Reporting

A report is useful only if it arrives while a decision can still change the outcome. Once the required date is missed, the choices become familiar and expensive: expediting, premium freight, emergency sourcing, resequencing work or escalating with the customer. Earlier warning does not guarantee success, but it gives management something valuable: options.

Figure 1 – The Delay Is Visible Before It Is Late (illustrative example)

In the example above, nothing is officially late when the first warning appears. What has changed is the amount of protection around the required date. Fabrication has moved, inspection is getting tighter, and the buffer that once absorbed normal variation is disappearing. Waiting for the final delivery date to turn red would mean ignoring the part of the schedule that was already speaking.

From Status to Signal

Most status reports answer a simple question: are we on time today? A stronger supply-chain view asks another one: is anything changing that could make us late tomorrow? That shift sounds small, but it changes where management attention goes.

The signals do not need to be sophisticated. Repeated milestone movement, a shrinking schedule buffer, approval queues, changing supplier promise dates, recurring defects, abnormal consumption or logistics disruption can all matter. No single signal proves that a delay will happen. The value comes from seeing the pattern and deciding whether it deserves attention.

A Warning Needs Context

There is also a danger in creating too many alerts. If every movement becomes a warning, people quickly stop listening. A useful warning therefore needs business context. It should tell us not only what changed, but what is exposed, how much room remains, who needs to look at it and what decision may be required.

For a practical early warning, five questions are usually enough:

•  Signal — what changed from the expected pattern?

•  Impact — which material, project, customer, cost or service outcome is exposed?

•  Cause — what is known, and what still needs validation?

•  Owner — who is accountable for investigating and responding?

•  Action — what decision or recovery step should happen next?

Figure 2 – The Decision-Ready Early Warning

Supply-chain information usually develops in stages. We first describe what happened, then understand why. With reliable history and context, we can begin to estimate what may happen next. The point is not prediction for its own sake; it is getting to a better decision sooner.

Supply intelligence develops in stages. We first need to understand what happened, then why it happened. With reliable data and context, we can begin to anticipate what may happen next — and, most importantly, decide what to do while there is still time to influence the outcome.

Figure 3 – Four Levels of Supply Intelligence

There is no need to jump straight to advanced prediction. If dates, supplier commitments and delay reasons are unreliable, a sophisticated model will only make unreliable information look more convincing.

What Makes Prediction Credible

Credible prediction starts with credible operations: common date definitions, updated supplier commitments, actual milestone timestamps and consistent exception reasons. Technology can build on that discipline; it cannot replace it.

Where AI Can Strengthen Early Warning

This is an area where AI can be genuinely useful. A person may be tracking dozens or hundreds of orders, supplier updates and milestones at the same time. AI can help scan that volume, summarize updates, flag unusual movement, compare current patterns with previous outcomes and bring the items that deserve attention to the surface.

Generative AI can add another layer by explaining the warning in normal management language: what changed, what may be affected, what evidence supports the concern and what should be checked next. Predictive analytics may help identify the risk; generative AI can help people understand it faster.

But the distinction matters. A probability is not a fact, and an alert is not a decision. Supplier selection, commercial commitments, approvals and risk acceptance still need accountable human judgment. The purpose of AI here is not to remove people from the process. It is to help them see the important issue sooner.

Figure 4 – Human Judgment Inside the Early-Warning Loop

A Practical Example: Critical Project Material

Imagine a critical transformer accessory needed before energization. The supplier has not declared a delay and the final delivery date still looks achievable. But two fabrication milestones have moved, the inspection window has tightened, and the logistics buffer has fallen from 18 days to 6. On a conventional report, the line may still be green.

That is exactly where an early-warning view earns its value. Instead of waiting for a missed promise date, the team can challenge the recovery plan, protect an inspection slot, review the shipment mode, adjust site sequencing or escalate commercially. Not every warning will become a delay. That is fine. The point is to have the conversation while several recovery options still exist.

Avoiding the False Promise of Prediction

Prediction brings its own risk: false confidence. Supply chains are affected by engineering changes, supplier behavior, regulation, weather, logistics constraints and human decisions. No model will anticipate all of them. A risk score should therefore start a conversation, not end one.

The goal is not certainty. It is earlier, better-informed management of uncertainty.

What Supply Chain Leaders Can Do

•  Start with one critical workflow where late visibility has a measurable business impact.

•  Define the few signals that genuinely change management attention or action.

•  Protect data quality: dates, milestones, ownership and exception reasons must be reliable.

•  Measure remaining buffer and trend, not only current status.

•  Connect every warning to an owner, response window and escalation path.

•  Use AI to prioritize and explain risk, while keeping accountable decisions with people.

•  Review false alarms and missed risks so the warning logic improves over time.

Supply Intelligence Reflection

For me, the more useful question is no longer simply, “What is late?” It is, “What is becoming late?” That change moves the discussion from explaining yesterday's problem toward protecting tomorrow's outcome.

Most organizations already hold more operational data than they can comfortably review. The challenge is turning that data into something people can act on. A warning that arrives after the problem is reporting. A warning that nobody owns is noise. A warning that arrives early, makes sense and reaches the right owner can change the outcome.

That is the shift from visibility to foresight: not pretending we can know the future, but creating enough warning to influence it.

Closing Perspective

Resilience is often discussed in terms of how quickly a supply chain recovers after disruption. But recovery is only one side of the story. The ability to recognize developing risk before the disruption fully lands can be just as important.

So the leadership question evolves again. It is no longer only, “Can we see our supply chain?” It becomes: “Can we recognize when the pattern is changing, and can we act while we still have choices?”

What has been the most useful early warning in your experience: a supplier's behavior, milestone drift, approval delay, inventory movement, logistics pressure, or something else? I would be interested to hear what has actually worked in practice.

Signals. Context. Foresight. Action.

title: FROM PROCESS TO PERFORMANCE: WHY A GREEN DASHBOARD CAN STILL MEAN LATE MATERIAL
excerpt: Most of us have sat in this meeting: the PR was processed on time, the RFQ went out on time, the PO was released inside target, every KPI is green, and the material is still going to arrive late. A process can be documented, measured and reported, and…
imageAlt: FROM PROCESS TO PERFORMANCE: WHY A GREEN DASHBOARD CAN STILL MEAN LATE MATERIAL
bodyHtml:
Most of us have sat in this meeting: the PR was processed on time, the RFQ went out on time, the PO was released inside target, every KPI is green, and the material is still going to arrive late. A process can be documented, measured and reported, and still not perform. The difference is whether the organization can see how work moves, where it waits, and which decision should follow.

Executive Insight

In Article 5, the focus was on designing workflows so people can understand and execute the Supply Chain process consistently. This article takes the next step: connecting those workflows to measurable results and to management action.

Supply Chain performance is rarely determined by one department or one KPI. It emerges from a sequence of handoffs: requirements become specifications, specifications become sourcing events, sourcing decisions become commitments, commitments become supplier and logistics actions, and those actions ultimately affect availability, project delivery, cost and customer outcomes.

The practical challenge is therefore not simply to measure activity. It is to connect workflow stages to meaningful measures, identify exceptions early, and create a management response before a local delay becomes a wider business problem.

Why Activity Does Not Equal Performance

A purchase request can be processed on time while the overall delivery outcome is already at risk. An RFQ can be issued quickly while the requirement behind it is incomplete. A purchase order can be released within the target cycle time after a technical approval has consumed the critical schedule buffer.

Activity tells us what a function completed. Performance asks whether the workflow produced the business result that was required. Nobody in the example below did their job badly. The time simply disappeared in the gap between jobs.

Figure 1 – Every Task on Time, Material Still Late (illustrative example)

Figure 1 – Every Task on Time, Material Still Late (illustrative example)

This is why many delays are created between functions rather than inside a single function. The handoff between Engineering and Procurement, Procurement and Finance, Procurement and suppliers, or Logistics and the project can matter more than any individual task. A department view shows who performed the work. It rarely shows who owned the wait.

The Workflow Is the Real Unit of Performance

A department view groups activities by responsibility. A workflow view follows the outcome across those responsibilities. Both are necessary, but they answer different questions: the first asks who performs the task; the second asks what must happen, in what sequence, with what information, decision and evidence, for the required outcome to be achieved.

This changes how performance should be measured. Instead of creating a separate KPI for every activity, organizations can connect a smaller set of measures to the points where work can slow, fail, change or create risk. For each critical workflow, leaders should be able to answer six questions:

•  Trigger — what starts the workflow, and what must be available before it starts?

•  Owner — who is accountable for keeping it moving?

•  Handoff — what must one function provide before the next function can proceed?

•  Decision gate — where is approval, technical acceptance, commercial selection or risk acceptance required?

•  Exception path — what happens when the normal route no longer applies?

•  Output — what result is produced, and how does it support the next stage?

If these answers are not visible, another dashboard is unlikely to help.

From KPI to Decision

A KPI becomes more valuable when it is connected to context and action. “PO cycle time: 38 days” is accurate, but on its own it only tells management how long the process took.

Add context and the conversation changes. 21 of those 38 days were spent waiting for technical approval. It affected one equipment package. The Engineering lead owns the approval. The action is to escalate today and close it by Friday. Same data, completely different management discussion.

Figure 2 – The Decision-Ready KPI

Finding the First Point of Delay

One of the most common reporting problems is treating the visible symptom as the root cause. A late delivery may be recorded as a supplier-performance problem even when the first delay occurred much earlier and the supplier inherited it.

A workflow-based review traces the event backward. Was the requirement complete? Was the specification released? Were approvals available? Was the purchase order released on time? Did the supplier receive the correct information? Did fabrication and inspection move as committed? Did logistics have enough time left to protect the required date?

Fixing the last symptom usually means expediting. Fixing the first point of delay means the same problem is not expedited again next quarter.

The Performance Chain

Supply performance can be viewed as a connected chain of five layers: process, workflow, measurement, decision and improvement. Weakness at any layer reduces the value of the next. Many organizations are strong at the first layer and thinner at the last three: they document well, and then rely on hope.

Figure 3 – Five Layers of Supply Performance

From Dashboard to Management Action

A dashboard should not become another screen that people review without changing anything. Its purpose is to make exceptions visible and shorten the distance between information and action.

A practical management rhythm can be simple: review the current exceptions, investigate the cause, decide the response, assign ownership, track the result and capture the learning. This creates a feedback loop rather than a static reporting process.

Where AI Can Strengthen the Model

Artificial Intelligence can add value once the workflow and data foundation are sufficiently clear. It can summarize procurement activity, identify unusual patterns, compare supplier performance, draft KPI commentary from structured data, highlight exceptions and help management interpret large volumes of information.

The important distinction is between AI assistance and autonomous decision-making. AI can reduce the effort required to understand a situation, but accountable people should retain control over commercial commitments, supplier decisions, approvals and risk acceptance. AI shortens the time to understanding. A person still owns the decision.

A Practical Example: Critical Project Material

Consider a critical long-lead item required for a project. A conventional report shows the purchase order as released and the supplier committed to a delivery date. It looks fine.

A workflow view connects the required date with specification release, PO release, fabrication milestones, inspection, logistics and expected site arrival. If a milestone moves beyond its agreed threshold, the exception is surfaced while there is still room to act: supplier action, inspection acceleration, logistics adjustment, alternative routing or escalation to the right stakeholder.

Figure 4 – Critical Material Workflow and Early Intervention (illustrative example)

The management question changes from “Why is the material late?” to “Which milestone has moved, what caused the movement, what is the downstream exposure, and who owns the recovery action?” The first question is asked at the site gate. The second is asked while something can still be done.

What Supply Chain Leaders Can Do

•  Map the critical end-to-end workflows before expanding the KPI library.

•  Measure elapsed time and waiting time, not only completed transactions.

•  Assign clear ownership to handoffs and exception points.

•  Connect every threshold to a specific management action.

•  Use dashboards to surface exceptions rather than overwhelm users with transactions.

•  Introduce AI where it improves interpretation, visibility or decision support.

•  When the same exception keeps returning, redesign the process instead of expediting it again.

Supply Intelligence Reflection

Across project-based and operational environments, one pattern keeps repeating: the biggest weaknesses are often found between functions, not inside them. Each team can follow its procedure correctly and still be surprised by the result, because nobody was measuring the handoff.

The question is not whether an organization has KPIs. The more important question is whether those KPIs are connected to the work that creates the result. When measurement is disconnected from workflow, reporting mainly describes the past. When it is connected, it can influence the next decision.

That is the shift from process to performance: making the flow visible, making the measurement meaningful, and using evidence to improve the next cycle.

Closing Perspective

Strong Supply Chain performance does not come from process documentation alone, and it does not come from technology alone. It comes from connecting people, processes, data, decisions and accountability around the outcomes the business needs.

The real leadership question is therefore not “Do we have KPIs?” It is: “Can we see where our work waits, and do we know who acts when it does?”

Where do delays in your organization actually start: inside a function, or between two of them? I would value your perspective in the comments.

Visibility. Measurement. Decisions. Continuous improvement.

title: THE POWER OF FLOW: DESIGNING SUPPLY CHAIN WORKFLOWS FOR BETTER PROCESS UNDERSTANDING & EXECUTION
excerpt: A good process manual tells people what the process is. A well-designed workflow goes a step further by showing how the work actually moves.
imageAlt: THE POWER OF FLOW: DESIGNING SUPPLY CHAIN WORKFLOWS FOR BETTER PROCESS UNDERSTANDING & EXECUTION
bodyHtml:
A good process manual tells people what the process is. A well-designed workflow goes a step further by showing how the work actually moves. A flowchart makes that movement easier to see and understand. Together, they help turn documented procedures into something people can follow and execute consistently.

Executive Insight

Supply Chain connects planning, sourcing, supplier management, purchasing, logistics, warehousing, inventory, quality and the flow of information required to make the whole system work. In many organizations, however, these processes still depend heavily on personal experience, informal instructions and “the way we usually do it” to keep the work moving.

A department manual can help, but a manual alone does not create process discipline. The stronger objective is to translate policies and responsibilities into practical workflows: clear triggers, defined ownership, decision points, handoffs, required records, exception paths and measurable outputs.

This matters because supply-chain work crosses organizational boundaries. Planning establishes demand and requirements. Purchasing translates approved requirements into commercial execution and coordinates with suppliers and logistics. Logistics hands materials to warehouses or operations. Finance, Quality, Engineering, Projects and other functions influence decisions along the way. A process document that stops at the department boundary is often technically complete but operationally incomplete. This piece focuses specifically on the processes Supply Chain owns end-to-end; Finance, HR, Engineering and Project teams are referenced only at their points of interface with Supply Chain, not as full department workflows in their own right.

Figure 1 – From Department Knowledge to Repeatable Workflow

Why Manuals Alone Do Not Create Process Discipline

A manual often answers what the organization expects. A workflow must go one step further and make the work executable. It should help a new employee, an experienced specialist, an approver and an auditor understand the same process in substantially the same way.

A useful test is simple: when a process starts, can the person responsible answer the following questions without relying on informal memory?

•   What triggers the process, and what information must be available before it starts?

•   Who owns the next action, who provides input, and who has the authority to decide?

•   What happens when the requirement is incomplete, urgent, changed or outside the normal route?

•   What system record, document or evidence proves that the step was completed correctly?

If these answers are not visible, the organization may have documentation but still operate through individual knowledge. That creates inconsistency, longer onboarding, avoidable rework and higher key-person risk.

From Activities to End-to-End Processes

Many departments document their own activities: create RFQ, issue PO, arrange shipment, receive material, update stock, process invoice. These statements describe tasks, but they do not explain how the tasks connect to the business outcome.

End-to-end process design should start with the required outcome and then look across the functions involved in delivering it. For example, material availability is not a Procurement output alone. It depends on planning accuracy, specification quality, supplier capability, approval timing, logistics execution, receiving discipline, inventory visibility and operational need.

The Supply Chain Process Is the Real Unit of Design

A stronger manual organizes information around the flow of work rather than only around the organization chart. Functions still retain professional responsibilities, but the workflow shows where one function’s output becomes another function’s input.

Figure 2 – Process View vs. Department View

What a Good Supply Chain Workflow Must Define

A workflow goes beyond a flowchart: it is a practical control design connecting people, decisions, data, systems and outputs. A complete workflow should make the following visible:

•   Trigger — the event that starts the process and the conditions required before work begins.

•   Inputs — the minimum information, specification, budget, forecast, stock data or supporting records required.

•   Process owner — the person accountable for keeping the workflow moving, even when several functions perform activities.

•   Functional responsibilities — the roles of Planning, Procurement, Supplier Management, Logistics, Warehouse, Inventory, Quality, Finance, Projects and other stakeholders as applicable.

•   Decision gates — the points where approval, technical acceptance, commercial selection, risk acceptance or escalation is required.

•   Controls and evidence — the checks, system transactions, approvals and records that demonstrate compliance and traceability.

•   Exceptions and escalation — the route for urgent requirements, failed suppliers, quality issues, delays, changes or other non-standard situations.

•   Output and handoff — what is produced, who receives it, by when, and what starts the next stage.

The Handoff Is Where Process Becomes Real

A process may look efficient on paper and still fail at its handoffs. The reason is that organizations often define responsibility within departments but leave the interface between departments implicit.

Figure 3 – Cross-Functional Handoff Requirements

The practical lesson is simple: do not only ask, “Who performs this step?” Ask, “What must be true before the next person can start without having to reconstruct the story?”

Designing the Supply Chain Manual Architecture

A useful department manual does not need to be one long document trying to describe every detail. It should be a controlled architecture in which each layer serves a different purpose. This makes the manual easier to use, maintain and connect with training, systems and audit evidence.

Figure 4 – Supply Chain Documentation Architecture

1. Policy and Principles

The policy layer establishes the boundaries: ethical expectations, authority, segregation of duties, sourcing principles, inventory principles, supplier governance, quality requirements, compliance obligations and other non-negotiable rules.

2. End-to-End Process

The process layer explains the intended business flow. It should show how demand or need becomes an executed outcome across functions, rather than describing each department in isolation.

3. SOP / Workflow

The SOP or workflow layer translates the process into execution. It should identify owners, sequence, decision gates, approvals, records, system actions, timing expectations and escalation paths.

4. Work Instructions

Work instructions explain the detailed method for a specific activity: for example, how to create a supplier record, complete a stock transaction, prepare a shipping document set or perform a defined inspection step.

5. Forms, System Fields and Records

The final layer creates the evidence. Templates, checklists, ERP fields, registers, approvals and retained records should support the workflow rather than create a parallel administrative system.

This structure also makes change management easier. A policy change should not require rewriting every work instruction, and a system enhancement should not silently change a policy. Each layer should have its own owner, review cycle and change-control logic.

Build the Workflow Around the Supply Chain, Not the Silo

A broader Supply Chain manual should connect the major flows that keep the business operating. The exact design will differ between manufacturing, services, retail, construction, EPC, healthcare and other environments, but the principle is consistent: the process should follow the movement of demand, information, materials and accountability.

Figure 5 – End-to-End Supply Chain Workflow

One Flow, Different Functional Expertise

An end-to-end workflow does not mean that every function performs every step. Planning remains accountable for demand and supply balancing where applicable. Purchasing translates approved requirements into commercial execution and coordinates with the relevant sourcing and supplier-management activities. Supplier Management monitors supplier performance and risk. Logistics controls movement and documentation. Warehousing and Inventory protect availability and record accuracy. Quality protects conformity. Finance maintains financial discipline and exposure visibility. The workflow is what connects these responsibilities into one controlled business flow.

Do Not Document the Normal Path Only

Real supply chains rarely operate entirely within the normal route. A supplier may miss a commitment. A project may accelerate. A specification may change. A shipment may be delayed. A quality issue may stop receipt. A critical requirement may become urgent. A strong manual makes these exceptions part of the design instead of leaving people to improvise when pressure is highest.

For each major exception, the workflow should identify the trigger, immediate containment action, decision authority, escalation route, required evidence and conditions for returning to the controlled process. This is where process documentation starts to support operational resilience.

Decision Gates and Exceptions: Where Control Meets Speed

Good governance does not mean adding an approval to every step. It means placing the right decision at the right point, with enough information for the person responsible to make a sound decision and enough control to protect the business.

A workflow should distinguish between execution steps and decision gates. Execution moves the work forward. A decision gate changes the route, commits resources, accepts risk, approves a supplier or confirms an outcome.

Figure 6 – Normal Workflow and Exception Path

Examples of Decision Gates Across Supply Chain

Figure 7 – Decision Gates Across Supply Chain

Digital Systems Should Execute the Workflow, Not Define It by Accident

ERP and workflow platforms are powerful when the business process is already clear. System configuration can then reinforce approval routing, required fields, status visibility, document retention and performance reporting. The opposite can also happen: the current system screens become the de facto process, and inefficient steps remain simply because “that is how the system works.”

What a Strong Supply Chain Manual Requires

•   A clear process architecture covering the major supply-chain flows, not only individual departmental tasks.

•   Defined ownership for every stage, including cross-functional handoffs and escalation responsibility.

•   Simple workflows that people can follow under normal conditions and under operational pressure.

•   Decision rights and approval thresholds aligned to value, risk, criticality, complexity and urgency.

•   Standard templates, checklists, system fields and records that reinforce the workflow instead of duplicating it.

•   Version control, document ownership, review dates and change-management discipline.

•   Performance measures that connect process execution to service, cost, inventory, delivery, supplier performance, risk and working capital outcomes.

None of this is about producing more documents for their own sake. The real goal is to reduce ambiguity, shorten the learning curve, protect control points and make the organization less dependent on individual memory.

What Supply Chain Leaders Can Do

•   Start by mapping five to ten critical end-to-end processes before writing large volumes of departmental procedures.

•   Identify every major handoff and define the information, timing and acceptance criteria required at that interface.

•   Separate policy, process, SOP, work instruction and evidence so each document has one clear purpose.

•   Design exception and escalation routes while the process is being created, not after the first failure.

•   Link workflows to ERP transactions, master data, forms and KPIs so the documented process and actual execution remain aligned.

•   Train people on the flow of work and decision logic, not only on where documents are stored.

•   Review workflows periodically using performance data, audit findings, user feedback and operational lessons.

Reality Check

Figure 8 – Reality Check: Assumption vs. Reality

Supply Intelligence Reflection

Across project-based, shared-services and operational environments, I have noticed one pattern repeatedly: processes become harder to manage when too much knowledge lives in people rather than in the operating system of the department. The strongest teams make the normal route, decision rights and exception paths clear enough that professional judgement can be applied where it creates value.

My experience has reinforced that the biggest weaknesses are often found between functions, not inside them. A Purchasing team can follow its procedure correctly and still face delays because requirements, technical approvals, supplier information, logistics or receiving records are not aligned. This is why a Supply Chain manual should not only document what each function does. It should also show how work moves between functions through clear workflows, handoffs, decision points and exception paths.

A good process manual tells people what the process is. A well-designed workflow shows how the process moves, while a flowchart makes that movement visible and easier to understand. Together, they turn documented procedures into processes that people can follow and execute consistently.

That is why I see the department manual not simply as a reference book, but as part of the Supply Chain operating model — connecting standards, workflows, responsibilities and execution.

Closing Perspective

A strong Supply Chain manual should not simply tell people what the organization expects. It should make the flow of work visible — who acts, who decides, what happens next, what evidence is created, and what changes when the normal path breaks. Manuals provide the structure; workflows provide the logic of movement; and flowcharts make that logic visible.

The real leadership question is therefore not “Do we have SOPs?” It is: “Can our Supply Chain function understand, execute and improve its processes consistently, transparently and resiliently without relying on individual memory?”

Standards. Handoffs. Controls. One repeatable Supply Chain.

title: ARTICLE 4 | BEYOND REPORTING LINES: DESIGNING THE RIGHT SUPPLY CHAIN OPERATING MODEL
excerpt: Supply Chain creates its greatest value when it is positioned as a strategic business function connecting commercial decisions with operational delivery. Executive Insight Supply Chain is broader than Procurement.
imageAlt: ARTICLE 4 | BEYOND REPORTING LINES: DESIGNING THE RIGHT SUPPLY CHAIN OPERATING MODEL
bodyHtml:
Supply Chain creates its greatest value when it is positioned as a strategic business function connecting commercial decisions with operational delivery.

Executive Insight

Supply Chain is broader than Procurement. Procurement is one important domain within the wider supply chain system, alongside planning, logistics, inventory, supplier management, warehousing, quality, and related disciplines. Yet organizations often design these responsibilities through reporting lines rather than through the decisions they need to make together.

The key question is therefore not simply, "Who does the Supply Chain or Procurement Department report to?" It is: "Who has the authority to make supply chain and procurement decisions, and are that decision rights designed appropriately?" This distinction matters because not every organization has a department named Supply Chain—many have only a Procurement department, with logistics, warehousing, or inventory sitting elsewhere. The question is about the function, not the department label.

Across centralized, shared services, civil contracting, and project-based environments, different structures can work effectively. The lesson is not that one structure is universally superior. The lesson is that the operating model must fit the business model and make authority visible.

Figure 1 – From Reporting Line to Business Accountability

Why the Operating Model Matters

A Supply Chain operating model defines how the wider function is organized, how responsibilities are divided, how decisions move across departments, and how Supply Chain interacts with Finance, Projects, Operations, Engineering, Sales, and senior management.

A weak model creates two opposite problems. Supply Chain may become a transactional service asked to execute decisions already made elsewhere. Or it may be given broad authority without enough connection to operational priorities, financial controls, or business realities. Neither extreme creates sustainable value.

The objective is not to maximize Supply Chain control. It is to create the right balance between business ownership, professional expertise, speed, governance, visibility, and accountability.

Supply Chain and Procurement: Clarifying the Relationship

Supply Chain and Procurement are often used interchangeably, but they are not the same thing. Supply Chain is the broader function; Procurement is a commercially critical domain within it. This distinction matters when designing an operating model because sourcing authority, logistics ownership, inventory decisions, supplier management, and quality responsibilities may sit differently across organizations.

Reporting Line, Functional Authority and Decision Rights

A formal reporting line answers: who is the organizational manager? Functional authority answers: who sets policy, standards, delegation rules, supplier governance, and professional expectations? Decision authority answers: who can approve the commitment? These can be different people or functions.

Supply Chain may report to Finance while operating under a group framework. It may report to Operations or directly to the CEO while Finance retains budget and financial control authority. In a project organization, Project Management may hold significant commercial decision rights while Supply Chain retains responsibility for sourcing, market engagement, supplier strategy, and professional challenges.

The practical decision-making line is visible through approval matrices, contract ownership, budget authority, technical acceptance, and escalation routes. When these rights are clear, Supply Chain can challenge constructively, business leadership can decide with full information, and Finance can understand the consequences. When rights are unclear, organizations experience duplicated approvals, delayed sourcing, and decisions made without the full commercial picture.

The Supply Chain Operating Model Spectrum

There is no universal Supply Chain operating model. The right model depends on the business model, size, geography, category complexity, operational or project intensity, risk, maturity, and the speed required by the organization. Centralized, decentralized, and hybrid models represent three established approaches to allocating authority, accountability, and execution.

Figure 2 – The Supply Chain Operating Model Spectrum

1. Centralized Supply Chain

A centralized model brings major Supply Chain activities under a common governance structure, potentially including planning, sourcing, Procurement, logistics, inventory, and supplier management. It can improve spend visibility, standardization, specialist capability, economies of scale, and commercial leverage.

Centralization is particularly attractive where business units have similar requirements, categories can be aggregated, and enterprise-wide control creates meaningful scale benefits. Its strength is integration: one function can see the trade-offs between cost, service, inventory, working capital, risk, and supply continuity rather than optimizing individual decisions in isolation.

2. Decentralized Supply Chain

A decentralized model gives business units, regions, or operations greater autonomy over Supply Chain decisions and execution. This can improve responsiveness, local market knowledge, and alignment with specific customers or operational requirements.

The trade-off is that greater autonomy can create duplicated capabilities, fragmented spend, inconsistent processes, and reduced enterprise-wide visibility. Decentralization therefore works best when local requirements genuinely differ and the benefits of responsiveness outweigh the potential loss of scale and standardization.

3. Hybrid Supply Chain

A hybrid model combines central governance with delegated execution. Strategic activities such as policy, category strategy, data standards, selected supplier relationships, and enterprise governance may remain centralized, while operational decisions are managed closer to the business, region, or project.

This model can provide a practical balance between economies of scale and local responsiveness. It is particularly useful where organizations operate across different markets, products, projects, or geographies and therefore need both enterprise-wide coordination and local flexibility.

The important point is that "hybrid" should not mean unclear. A strong hybrid model deliberately specifies what is centralized, what is delegated, who owns each decision, and how exceptions are escalated.


How to Select the Right Supply Chain Operating Model

The most important question is not "Which model is best?" but "Which model best fits how this organization creates value and manages risk?" The selection should be based on a structured assessment rather than organizational fashion or reporting-line preference.

Selecting the Model: A Practical Decision Test

A management team can test the operating model through seven questions:

·        Where does scale create measurable commercial leverage?

·        Where do requirements genuinely differ between business units, locations or projects?

·        Which decisions require specialist Supply Chain expertise or enterprise-wide visibility?

·        Which decisions require close operational or technical knowledge?

·        Where could excessive centralization slow delivery?

·        Where could excessive decentralization create fragmented spend, supplier risk or inconsistent governance?

·        What decision rights, systems and controls are required to make the chosen model work?

The answers do not need to produce a single answer for the whole function. An organization can centralize strategic categories and supplier governance while delegating routine execution. It can also use different levels of authority for different categories based on value, risk, criticality and complexity.

Operating Models by Organizational Context

The same model does not need to be applied identically across every type of organization. The operating context matters.

These are not fixed rules. They are starting points for design. The final model should reflect the organization’s actual scale, complexity, risk, supply market and decision-making needs.

Project-Based Organizations: Applying the Operating Model

Projects are one important context in which operating-model choices become visible. Project organizations carry time-bound delivery commitments, technical dependencies, client obligations and schedule consequences. These characteristics can justify greater local authority — but they do not automatically require a fully decentralized Supply Chain function.

Project-Level Authority: Speed with Clear Boundaries

Project teams should own the business outcome: what is required, when it is required, the technical or functional priorities, and the delivery consequence of delay. Supply Chain/Procurement should bring market intelligence, sourcing strategy, supplier capability assessment, commercial analysis, and negotiation expertise. Finance and governance functions provide budget and control discipline.

The key is to distinguish business ownership from professional expertise. The project or business owner can define the need, confirm priorities, and accept the outcome within approved authority, while Supply Chain leads or supports market engagement, competition, negotiation strategy, supplier evaluation, and supplier-risk analysis.

This distinction prevents a common misunderstanding: Supply Chain does not need to own the business requirement to add strategic value to the decision.

The Supply Chain Decision-Rights Triangle

Major Supply Chain decisions rarely belong to one function alone. They sit at the intersection of Supply Chain, Business/Operations, and Finance/Governance.

Figure 3 – The Supply Chain Decision-Rights Triangle

Supply Chain contributes market intelligence, sourcing strategy, supplier capability assessment, negotiation expertise, and commercial challenge through Procurement, alongside logistics, inventory, and quality governance. Business/Operations contributes the requirement, technical priorities, service expectations, schedule, and accountability for the outcome. Finance/Governance contributes budget discipline, financial exposure management, controls, risk oversight, and compliance.

Business/Operations is intentionally broad: depending on the requirement, it can include Projects, Engineering, Production, Maintenance, HR, Administration, IT, Facilities, and other functional owners.

Delegation of Authority: Speed Without Losing Control

Delegation of Authority (DoA) is one of the most important practical mechanisms in an operating model. Not every purchase needs the same level of management attention. Routine, lower-risk purchases can be delegated, while strategic, high-value or high-risk commitments require higher approval.

·        Define monetary thresholds and approval levels clearly.

·        Separate routine purchasing authority from strategic sourcing and contract authority.

·        Consider risk, criticality and business impact — not only purchase value.

·        Define who can approve commercial deviations, exceptions and supplier selection.

·        Create clear escalation routes for urgent operational or project requirements.

·        Review delegated authority as spend profiles, projects and organizational structures change.

Business Functions and Indirect Supply Decisions

The operating-model question also applies outside projects. Departments may initiate indirect purchases because they own the operational requirement. HR, Facilities, IT, Administration, Production, Engineering, Maintenance and other functions may understand the requirement best, while Supply Chain provides appropriate commercial, sourcing and supplier-management support.

The level of Supply Chain involvement does not need to be identical for every category. Strategic, high-value or high-risk requirements may require stronger central governance, while lower-risk or routine requirements may be managed closer to the business within defined policies and delegated authority.

The key governance questions are straightforward: who owns the requirement, when is Supply Chain involvement mandatory, who approves the commitment, who owns the supplier relationship, when is a PO or contract required, and how are exceptions controlled?

Making the Operating Model Work End-to-End

Whatever model is selected, responsibilities must remain connected across the supply chain. The objective is not to move every decision into Supply Chain. It is to make decision rights clear, proportionate and commercially sound from need identification through supplier delivery.

Figure 4 – End-to-End Supply Chain Governance

What a Strong Operating Model Requires

·        Clear decision rights between Supply Chain, business functions and Finance/Governance.

·        A deliberate balance between central expertise and business responsiveness.

·        Defined Delegation of Authority aligned to value, risk, criticality and complexity.

·        Common policies, data standards and supplier governance where enterprise consistency creates value.

·        Early Supply Chain visibility of budgets, specifications, schedules, market conditions and commercial strategy.

·        Business ownership of requirements without fragmented purchasing or unmanaged supplier risk.

·        Performance measures that connect Supply Chain activity to cost, risk, delivery, working capital, service and supplier outcomes.

The strongest model is therefore not necessarily the most centralized model. Nor is it the model that gives every project or department maximum autonomy. It is the model that places each decision at the level where it can be made with the right combination of expertise, information, accountability and speed.

What Supply Chain and Procurement Leaders Can Do

·        Map reporting lines, functional authority and actual decision rights separately.

·        Identify which categories and decisions genuinely benefit from centralization.

·        Define where business units, operations or projects need delegated authority.

·        Document who owns the requirement, sourcing strategy, supplier selection, contract approval and commercial risk.

·        Use hybrid structures deliberately where central expertise and business responsiveness are both required.

·        Give Supply Chain early visibility of budgets, schedules, specifications and commercial strategy.

·        Review the operating model periodically as the organization, spend profile and risk environment change.

Supply Intelligence Reflection

Supply Chain operating models are often discussed in terms of centralized, decentralized, shared services, or project-based structures. In my experience, a strong and well-positioned Supply Chain function provides the greatest value when it has enterprise-wide visibility, clear decision rights, and sufficient authority to influence the commercial and operational decisions that shape business performance. What matters is whether Supply Chain has sufficient authority, visibility, and governance to connect business ownership, functional expertise, financial control, and delivery accountability.

Closing Perspective

A strong Supply Chain operating model should position Supply Chain as a strategic enterprise function with the authority and visibility required to influence commercial and operational outcomes.

The real leadership question is not simply whether Supply Chain should be centralized, but how centralized authority should be designed: which decisions require enterprise-level control, which should remain close to the business, and what governance framework is required to connect the two.

Structure. Authority. Governance. One connected Supply Chain.

About Supply Intelligence

Supply Intelligence is a professional knowledge-sharing initiative dedicated to exploring Supply Chain and Procurement, Artificial Intelligence, digital transformation, sustainability and project delivery in complex business environments. Its objective is to encourage meaningful discussion, challenge conventional thinking, and contribute to the continuous development of supply chain and procurement professionals through practical insights and evidence-based perspectives.

Originally published on LinkedIn by Raza Mustafa.

title: BEYOND COST SAVINGS: WHY PROCUREMENT AND FINANCE MUST WORK AS STRATEGIC PARTNERS
imageAlt: BEYOND COST SAVINGS: WHY PROCUREMENT AND FINANCE MUST WORK AS STRATEGIC PARTNERS
bodyHtml:
Different priorities. Complementary strengths. One business goal.

(Procurement creates commercial value. Finance protects financial value. Together, they drive sustainable business success.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Executive Insight

For many years, Procurement and Finance were treated as two separate support functions with different responsibilities and different priorities. Procurement was associated with sourcing and supplier negotiations, while Finance was associated with budgets, reporting and financial control. That description is increasingly incomplete.

Modern Procurement has moved far beyond the purchase order. In complex organisations, procurement professionals contribute to budgeting, forecasting, total cost of ownership, supplier financial assessment, contract strategy, inventory decisions, market intelligence, local content, risk management, sustainability and project delivery. Finance, meanwhile, does far more than approve budgets: it provides the financial framework through which organisations assess profitability, cash flow, capital allocation, compliance and performance.

The two functions therefore have different mandates, but they influence many of the same business outcomes. The real opportunity is not to make Procurement behave like Finance, or Finance behave like Procurement. It is to make their different perspectives work together.

Throughout my career across luxury goods, cosmetics, healthcare, construction, EPC and energy environments, I have seen the consequences of both approaches. When Procurement and Finance work independently, decisions can become optimised for one objective while creating unintended consequences elsewhere. When they work together, commercial decisions become more complete and business value becomes easier to see.

Why This Discussion Matters

The phrase “cost savings” is still deeply associated with Procurement. Savings are important, of course, but a procurement decision can influence far more than the purchase price. A supplier selected because of the lowest quotation may create a delivery problem. A payment term negotiated without considering supplier cash requirements may increase supply risk. An inventory reduction that looks attractive financially may weaken service levels. Conversely, a higher initial price may be justified when it reduces lifecycle cost, improves reliability or protects project delivery.

Finance faces a similar challenge from the opposite direction. A decision that improves short-term cash flow may not always be the best long-term commercial decision. Extending payment terms, reducing inventory or delaying expenditure can produce a positive financial indicator while placing pressure on suppliers, operations or project schedules.

This is why Procurement–Finance collaboration matters. The objective is not to eliminate different priorities. The objective is to bring those priorities into the same decision.

Different Priorities, One Business Goal

Procurement and Finance approach business decisions through different lenses. Neither perspective is inherently right or wrong; each protects a different part of the value equation.

The Traditional Disconnect Is Changing

The traditional view of Procurement as a transactional function no longer reflects the reality of modern supply management. Procurement teams increasingly participate before a purchase request is raised. They may contribute to demand planning, budget preparation, market testing, specification reviews, supplier development, contract strategy and risk analysis. In project environments, they may also monitor long-lead items, logistics constraints, supplier capacity and commercial exposure.

Organisational reporting lines also vary. In some SMEs, Procurement reports into Finance, while in other organisations it reports directly to the CEO, Managing Director or another executive sponsor. Either structure can work when roles, decision rights, controls and escalation routes are clear. Where Procurement sits within Finance, clear segregation of duties should still be maintained between sourcing, approval, contracting, receiving and payment. The key is not simply where Procurement sits on the organisation chart, but whether it has the authority and cross-functional access needed to protect commercial value while working effectively with Finance.

In Saudi Arabia, the procurement agenda can be broader still. Depending on the organisation and client requirements, procurement teams may need to consider local content objectives, supplier development, localisation, compliance requirements, market capability and other strategic considerations alongside price and delivery. These factors can materially affect how a sourcing decision should be evaluated.

Finance therefore needs procurement intelligence early, not only when an invoice reaches the accounts payable process. Procurement needs financial insight early as well, particularly when assessing affordability, cash flow, working capital and the financial consequences of commercial terms.

Procurement Is Already Part of the Financial Equation

A mature procurement function does not wait for Finance to tell it what the budget is. It helps Finance understand what the market can realistically deliver within that budget. Market intelligence can reveal whether an estimate is realistic, whether commodity movements may affect future cost, whether a specification is driving unnecessary expenditure, or whether an alternative sourcing strategy could reduce total cost.

Procurement also influences financial outcomes through decisions that may not appear as “savings” on a sourcing report. Payment terms affect cash flow. Order quantities affect working capital. Supplier reliability affects expediting and downtime. Contract clauses affect commercial exposure. Inventory decisions affect capital tied up in stock. Supplier financial health affects continuity risk.

This is why procurement performance should be viewed through a broader value lens. The strongest procurement leaders understand the financial consequences of commercial decisions and can explain those consequences in a language that Finance and senior management can use.

Finance Needs Procurement Intelligence Too

The relationship should not be one-directional. Finance benefits when Procurement provides reliable information about supply markets, supplier capability, contract commitments, pricing trends and operational risk.

For example, a Finance team may see a committed expenditure figure in an ERP system. Procurement can add the context behind that number: whether a supplier is strategically important, whether a quotation is still valid, whether a long-lead item is at risk, whether a contractual escalation clause may apply, or whether an alternative supplier is available. That context can materially improve forecasting and financial decision-making.

The best financial forecast is therefore not created by Finance alone. It is built from a combination of financial data and operational intelligence.

Where the Partnership Creates Value

Better budgeting: Procurement market intelligence can make budgets and estimates more realistic before commitments are made.

Total Cost of Ownership: Decisions can account for purchase price, logistics, installation, maintenance, quality, downtime and end-of-life considerations where relevant.

Working capital: Order quantities, inventory levels, payment terms and supplier arrangements can be considered together rather than in isolation.

Supplier risk: Commercial and financial information can be combined to identify suppliers whose failure could affect cost, continuity or project delivery.

Forecasting: Procurement commitments, market trends and supplier lead times provide valuable inputs to financial forecasts.

Contract management: Commercial clauses, variations, claims, escalation mechanisms and payment structures can be evaluated with both financial and procurement perspectives.

Local content and sustainability: Strategic sourcing can support localisation and sustainability objectives while Finance evaluates their financial implications and long-term value.

Project profitability: Procurement decisions can be connected directly to project cost, schedule, cash flow and margin rather than being measured only at purchase-order level.

The Procurement Lifecycle and Finance: A Shared View

The partnership should begin before sourcing and continue beyond contract award. A useful way to think about it is as a shared decision cycle.

1. Planning — Procurement brings market intelligence, demand information and supplier capability; Finance provides budget, cash flow and investment parameters.

2. Sourcing — Procurement leads commercial strategy and supplier engagement while Finance helps assess affordability, financial impact and business case assumptions.

3. Evaluation — Procurement assesses technical, commercial and supply considerations; Finance helps evaluate total financial impact and relevant financial risks.

4. Contracting — Both functions consider payment terms, guarantees, liabilities, escalation, currency exposure and other commercial consequences.

5. Delivery — Procurement monitors supplier performance, delivery and changes; Finance monitors commitments, cash flow and actual-versus-budget performance.

6. Close-out and learning — Both functions review final cost, supplier performance, claims, lessons learned and opportunities for future improvement.

Digitalization: Connecting Procurement and Finance Through Data

Digitalization provides another important bridge between Procurement and Finance. Modern ERP platforms, spend analytics, e-procurement tools and integrated dashboards can give both functions a shared view of commitments, supplier performance, budgets, inventory, payment status and market trends. Instead of waiting for month-end reports, leaders can use near real-time data to identify deviations, assess exposure and make faster commercial decisions.

Artificial Intelligence can take this further. AI-enabled analytics can identify unusual spending patterns, forecast demand, highlight supplier-risk signals, support contract analysis and help predict potential cost or delivery issues before they become significant. The real value, however, is not the technology itself. It is the ability to connect Procurement's market and supplier intelligence with Finance's financial data so that both functions are working from the same facts. Digitalization should therefore not create another system owned by one department; it should create a shared intelligence layer that turns data into better business decisions.

DIGITAL INSIGHT  |  The future is not Procurement versus Finance—it is Procurement + Finance + Data.

Beyond Cost Savings: The Modern Value Equation

One of the most important changes in procurement leadership is moving from a narrow savings mindset to a broader value mindset. A lower purchase price is not automatically a lower business cost. Likewise, a higher initial price is not automatically poor value.

The right question is often: “What option creates the best overall business outcome when cost, quality, time, risk, cash flow and strategic requirements are considered together?”

This does not make savings irrelevant. It makes savings more meaningful. A saving that is achieved without damaging quality, delivery, supplier resilience or project performance is valuable. A saving that creates a larger cost elsewhere is simply cost transfer.

Lessons Across Industries

The Procurement–Finance relationship looks different across industries, but the underlying principle remains remarkably consistent.

Luxury Goods and Retail: In luxury retail, procurement decisions can affect product availability, inventory investment, supplier relationships and ultimately customer experience. Finance is naturally concerned with margins, working capital and inventory performance. Procurement must therefore think beyond unit price and understand how supply decisions affect the economics of the brand and the customer.

Cosmetics: In cosmetics and beauty businesses, packaging, ingredients, quality, compliance, lead times and supplier innovation can all influence commercial performance. Finance must understand why a particular sourcing decision may carry a higher initial cost but reduce quality, supply or regulatory risk. Procurement, in turn, must understand the financial limits within which the business operates.

Healthcare: Healthcare procurement adds another dimension: availability and compliance can be critical. A procurement decision cannot be evaluated only through price when product quality, regulatory requirements and continuity of supply are involved. Finance provides the discipline needed to manage resources responsibly while Procurement protects operational availability.

Construction and EPC: In construction and EPC environments, the connection becomes especially visible. Long-lead materials, supplier capacity, payment terms, logistics, contract strategy, variations and delivery dates can influence project cash flow and profitability. A procurement decision made today can affect the project months later. This makes early coordination with Finance and Project Controls particularly important.

Saudi Energy Projects: In Saudi energy and infrastructure projects, procurement may also need to consider local content, supplier qualification, market capacity, compliance and project-specific requirements. These considerations can influence sourcing strategy, supplier selection and commercial evaluation. Finance adds the discipline of budget control, cash-flow planning and financial exposure. The combined view produces a stronger decision than either function can produce independently.

Supply Intelligence in Practice

Consider a major equipment package where two suppliers are technically acceptable. Supplier A offers the lower purchase price and more attractive headline savings. Supplier B is more expensive but offers stronger delivery assurance, better payment flexibility and a more robust local support structure.

A purely price-driven evaluation may favour Supplier A. A broader Procurement–Finance evaluation would ask additional questions: What is the cash-flow effect? What happens if Supplier A is late? What would the project cost if commissioning were delayed? Does Supplier B reduce logistics or support costs? Is the additional price justified by lower risk? What are the contractual protections? Does either option improve local content or supplier development objectives?

The answer may still be Supplier A. The important point is that the decision is now based on evidence rather than a single number.

This is where Procurement leadership matters. The procurement professional is not simply presenting quotations. The professional is helping management understand the commercial consequences of each option.

Reality Check

COMMON ASSUMPTION

REALITY

Procurement owns savings; Finance owns budgets.

Both functions influence financial value, but from different perspectives.

The lowest price is the best commercial result.

The best result considers TCO, risk, quality, delivery and strategic requirements.

Finance only needs Procurement data after a purchase order.

Early procurement intelligence improves budgets, forecasts and risk assessment.

Procurement only needs Finance when a budget is approved.

Financial understanding improves sourcing strategy, negotiation and commercial decisions.

Long payment terms are always good for cash flow.

They may help short-term cash flow but can increase supplier risk if poorly designed.

Practical Recommendations for Procurement Leaders & Organisations

For Procurement Leaders

  • Learn the language of Finance. Understand budgets, cash flow, working capital, margin, ROI, forecasts and financial exposure.
  • Invite Finance into strategic sourcing early, not only for approval. Early collaboration creates better decisions and fewer surprises.
  • Give Finance context, not just numbers. Explain supplier conditions, market movements, delivery risks and contractual commitments.
  • Measure value broadly. Track savings, but also consider cost avoidance, TCO, working capital, supplier performance, risk reduction, delivery and project outcomes.
  • Build common dashboards. Procurement and Finance should work from consistent definitions of spend, commitments, savings, forecasts and supplier exposure.
  • Challenge internal demand constructively. The strongest savings often come from specification, demand, standardisation or lifecycle decisions—not only supplier negotiation.
  • Protect supplier relationships. Financial discipline should not unintentionally create supply-chain fragility. Strategic suppliers are business partners, not simply payment recipients.

The Modern Procurement Leader

The modern procurement leader needs to be commercially strong, financially literate and operationally aware. Negotiation remains important, but it is only one part of the role. A senior procurement professional must understand how a sourcing decision affects the P&L, cash flow, working capital, project schedule, supplier ecosystem and long-term business strategy.

The same applies to Finance. Financial leadership becomes stronger when it understands the realities of supply markets, supplier capacity, lead times, logistics and commercial risk. Numbers become more useful when the organisation understands the operational story behind them.

This is where cross-functional leadership becomes a competitive advantage. Procurement and Finance do not need identical KPIs or identical responsibilities. They need enough shared understanding to make decisions that optimise the organisation rather than one department in isolation.

For Organisations

  1. Create joint Procurement–Finance reviews for major categories and projects.
  2. Agree common definitions for savings, cost avoidance, commitments and forecast impact.
  3. Include Procurement market intelligence in budgeting and forecasting cycles.
  4. Use TCO and risk-based evaluation for strategic purchases instead of price alone.
  5. Review payment terms alongside supplier financial health and supply criticality.
  6. Connect procurement performance with project and business outcomes.
  7. Develop procurement professionals' financial capability and finance professionals' supply-market awareness.
  8. Use technology and analytics to create a shared, trusted view of commercial and financial data.

Supply Intelligence Reflection

Different priorities do not have to create organisational boundaries. In fact, they can create stronger decisions when the perspectives are brought together.

Throughout my career across luxury goods, cosmetics, healthcare, construction, EPC and energy, I have seen procurement evolve from a transactional activity into a broader business function. The strongest procurement professionals I have worked with were not simply good negotiators. They understood the business behind the purchase.

They understood that a supplier decision could affect inventory. A contract could affect cash flow. A delivery delay could affect project timeline/profitability. A payment term could influence supplier resilience. A local-content requirement could influence sourcing strategy and a decision that looked attractive on paper could still create an unintended cost somewhere else.

That is why I believe the future of Procurement–Finance collaboration is not about one function taking ownership from the other. It is about combining two different forms of intelligence.

Procurement brings market intelligence, commercial judgement and supply-chain insight. Finance brings financial discipline, governance and performance perspective. When those capabilities are connected, organizations are better positioned to make decisions that are not only cheaper, but smarter. Different priorities. Complementary strengths. One business goal.

About Supply Intelligence

Supply Intelligence is a professional knowledge-sharing initiative dedicated to exploring procurement, supply chain management, Artificial Intelligence, digital transformation, sustainability and project delivery in complex business environments. The objective is to encourage meaningful discussion, challenge conventional thinking and contribute to the continuous development of procurement and supply chain professionals through practical insights and evidence-based perspectives.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ERP: PARTNERS, NOT COMPETITORS
